title: The bull, the fire, the swan, the bird teach Satyakama (4.5–4.8)
hook: sent off with four hundred thin cows, Satyakama is taught by the herd's bull, the evening fire, a swan and a diving bird

segments.voice: Yesterday: Satyakama, the boy who said I don't know at the teacher's door. Your line was truth is the qualification. Did you give a true answer where an easy one was waiting? Today also ends the first week of year two. Day three hundred thirty-six.

Satyakama has been accepted. You'd expect his first lesson to be a verse, a chant, a teaching by the fire. Instead his teacher picks out four hundred cows, thin and weak, and says: look after these. Satyakama doesn't complain. He says: I won't come back until they're a thousand. And he drives them off into the forest, and stays away for years. No teacher. No books. Just cows, grass, and the sky. And it's out there, alone, that the lessons start arriving, from teachers nobody would have chosen.
screen: `FOUR HUNDRED THIN COWS.` → `NOT BACK UNTIL A THOUSAND.` → `ALONE IN THE FOREST FOR YEARS.`

segments.voice: When the herd reaches a thousand, the bull speaks. Satyakama, we're a thousand now. Take us home. And let me tell you one quarter of Brahman, the great reality. The bull names the four directions, east, west, south, north, and calls that quarter the shining. Then the bull says the fire will tell him the next. That evening, Satyakama lights the fire and pens the cows, and the fire speaks: earth, the air between, the sky, the ocean. That quarter is the endless. The next evening, a swan flies down: fire, sun, moon, lightning. The luminous. The evening after, a diving water bird: breath, eye, ear, mind. The quarter that has a home. Four teachers, four quarters: the world around him, the world above, the lights, and his own body. He arrives at his teacher's house, and the teacher looks at him and says: your face shines like someone who knows Brahman. Who taught you? Satyakama answers: beings other than people. But please, teach me yourself. And his teacher does, and the text says nothing was left out. Now the week, looked at from the top. Day one, om, the essence of essences. Day two, the senses argue, and breath wins. Day three, dogs chanting for breakfast. Day four, a boy telling the truth at the door. Today, a bull, a fire, a swan and a bird. Five days in, the Chandogya keeps saying the same thing: the sacred is not locked in the ritual. It's in the breath, the truth, the herd and the evening fire.
screen: `THE BULL: THE FOUR DIRECTIONS.` · `THE FIRE, THE SWAN, THE DIVING BIRD.` · `YOUR FACE SHINES. WHO TAUGHT YOU?` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice listens for teachers. Sit and settle. Notice the direction you're facing, and the ones behind and beside you, the bull's quarter. Feel the ground and the air above it, the fire's quarter. Notice whatever light is around you, the swan's. Then come home to your breath, your eyes, your ears, your mind, the diving bird's. No need to hear any voices. Just let each one be a teacher for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
The bull. The first of Satyakama's four unlikely teachers, who names the four directions as the shining quarter of Brahman.
Your line: the whole world teaches. Today, let one unlikely thing teach you something, an animal, a kid, a stranger, the weather, and notice what it was. Day three hundred thirty-six.

screen: `DAY 336 COUNTS.` → `WEEK ONE OF YEAR TWO, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: UPAKOSALA AND THE FIRES.`

howItsDone: Many Hindus honor the natural world as full of the sacred: cows, rivers, fire and the directions all have places in daily worship, and teachers often tell Satyakama's story to show that learning can come from anywhere.

myth: Satyakama's teacher sent him off with a thousand cows
four hundred thin, weak cows. Satyakama vowed not to return until they were a thousand.
Satyakama asks his teacher to teach him anyway
even after the bull, fire, swan and bird, he asks to hear it from his teacher, and nothing is left out.
the teacher says Satyakama's face shines like a knower of Brahman
he can see it before Satyakama says a word.

fork.setup: you're Satyakama, home with a thousand cows. a bull, a fire, a swan and a bird have taught you. your teacher asks who taught you. what do you do next?
options: say you need no teacher now.
tell him the truth, and ask him to teach you himself.
claim you figured it all out alone.
fork.reveal: he says: beings other than people. then he asks his teacher to teach him anyway, and the teacher does, leaving nothing out.

original.note: Sanskrit haṃsa: swan or wild goose, the third of Satyakama's teachers. later a common image for the soul.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable where animals talk.
what it means: four quarters of Brahman, taught by the world itself: the directions, the worlds, the lights, and the body's senses.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 4.5–4.8, a fourfold teaching: the shining, the endless, the luminous, and the one with a home (ayatanavan); in 4.9 the teacher confirms it.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 4.5–4.8 (the bull, the fire, the swan, the diving bird)
Chandogya Upanishad 4.9 (your face shines; nothing left out)

notes: Week end (days 332–336, the first days of year two): look-back included in the teach.
Names of the four quarters: prakashavan (shining), anantavan (endless), jyotishman (luminous), ayatanavan (having a support/abode, rendered 'the one that has a home'). Confirm renderings.
The fourth teacher is the madgu, a diving water bird (often rendered 'diver' or 'cormorant'); kept as 'a diving water bird'.
'Years' in the forest: the text says he dwelt away for a number of years; confirm wording.
